newsitem.title: GERMANY: Soaring Deutsche Telekom demand worries banks.
newsitem.headline: Soaring Deutsche Telekom demand worries banks.

text.p: Nearly one and a half million German private investors have placed firm orders to buy at least 100 shares in Deutsche Telekom when the German phone giant goes public next week, the company said on Tuesday.

The enormous demand will guarantee that the $12 billion issue is oversubscribed several times but has managers of Europe's largest-ever share offering getting braced for a wave of investor discontent as the shares will be in short supply.

Around 3.1 million Germans signed up with the company's share information centre (AIF) to take advantage of discounted share prices and loyalty bonuses for holding shares three years. Nearly half of these have now placed orders.
"We are in the range of our expectations with orders from 40 to 50 percent of the AIF participants," Telekom spokesman Hans Ehnert told Reuters.

Orders for shares can be placed until Thursday. The company will float up to 690 million shares. Trade begins in Germany and New York on November 18 and a day later in Tokyo. The shares are expected to cost around 30 marks.
Around 70 percent of shares will be placed in Germany and divided up between individual and institutional investors.

Because of the heavy demand individuals who placed large orders for hundreds of shares could end up receiving only a fraction of their total orders, which could leave many individual investors disappointed.
Anticipating complaints from angry first-time investors, lead underwriter, Deutsche Bank AG, has set up a hot-line to try to ease the potential problem by offering advice.
"We presume that not every investor will be able to receive the full allotment," said bank spokesman Roland Weichert.

"We will offer specific consulting afterwards with investors who did not receive their full allocation to point out alternatives, such as buying Telekom shares on the market or making other investments."

Telekom's 100-million-mark ($67 million) advertising campaign has whipped up such interest in the issue that the financial community is hoping the issue could be a catalyst that sparks broad-based ownership of shares in Germany.
But hopes could be dashed if first-time investors feel that Telekom's slick TV ads promised more than they delivered.
The first rumblings of investor discontent began after Telekom unexpectedly topped up the issue on Monday with the placement of up to 115 million additional shares.

The Association for the Protection of Shareholders (DSW), Germany's largest shareholder's rights lobby, slammed Telekom for fattening the issue, saying it would weaken investor earnings potential and alienate first-time shareholders.
"The huge advertising success has led Telekom to seize the opportunity and ruthlessly exploit it," a DSW statement said.

The shareholders' lobby group said private investors who signed on early would see their dividends watered down and that the potential for a rise in Telekom's share price was reduced because institutional investors would receive extra shares.
Tight supply for institutional investors was expected to be the main factor that would drive Telekom's share price up soon after the offering.
DSW said Telekom's moves to take some of the wind out of the sails of its new shares "do not serve to build trust for new shareholders and damage Germany as a financial centre".
Deutsche Telekom, however, rejected the criticism. It said the additional shares would have little impact on share price developments and that it would not change dividend policy.
It is also not unusual for companies to add shares to an initial public offering shortly before the placement if demand exceeds expectations.
Sporting goods maker Adidas AG last year topped up its IPO with 4.6 million additional shares to 27.3 million just four days ahead of the issue.
"This kind of thing happens all the time with stock offerings," said Deutsche Bank's Weichert.
